messages.subject: Sumstats Flags
messages.body_plain:
To all,

I was working through a GWAS by subtraction and I am not sure what flags to use.

I was using Howard et al.'s 2019 depression GWAS excluding 23andMe - a meta analysis of UKB broad depression (analyzed de novo I think using BGENIE) and Wray et al's 2017 PGC depression GWAS (minus the UKB cohort to avoid duplication).  I cannot determine Wray's method of analysis from the published paper or supplement but her meta-analysis may have included Ripke et al's earlier PGC GWAS which used logistic regression.

Would Howard's meta-analysis GWAS then come under the category in the flow-chart of Meta-analysis of binary and continuous (as meta-analysis of GWASs using both logistics and linear regression) or some other category, for Sumstats flag?

Thanks for any help you can give me in this!

Dan

My understanding is that the broad depression phenotype still reflects a case/control trait just broadly defined (though i could see how the naming of the variable would lead someone to think that it reflects a continuous measure like from the PHQ-9 in UKB for example). messages.body_plain:
For summary statistics which have Z statistics (rather than effect sizes and standard errors, or odds ratio and standard errors) and p-values from METAL meta-analysis, how would you use the munge() function? It looks like the munge() function requires effect sizes/odds ratio and standard errors, and doesn't work if you have just Z statistics.

Also, if you have Z statistics from METAL from multiple binary traits (and not both binary and continuous traits together), in the sumstats() function would you do se.logit=F, OLS=T, and linprob=F and not state the sample/population prevalence (i.e., have them be NA)?

messages.subject: Re: Z statistics from meta-analysis for genomic SEM
messages.subject_clean: Z statistics from meta-analysis for genomic SEM
messages.body_plain:
Hi Lucy,

The munge function should work if you only have Z-statistics; it only requires that the effect column be signed (i.e., it is not the absolute value of Z-statistics). For the sumstats function, you do need an effect and standard error column. If you just have Z-statistics for binary traits you can back out the logistic beta and it's SE by calculating the SE as 1/sqrt(sum(eff_N/4)*MAF) and the logistic beta as Z/sqrt(sum(eff_N/4)*MAF). Where sum(eff_N/4) is the sum of the effective sample sizes  across the contributing cohorts (I think METAL automatically outputs a sum of effective sample sizes column that you could use for these equations). Then you would treat these just like they were a logistic beta and it's SE and set se.logit = T, OLS=F, and linprob=F.

Best,
  Andrew

Yes, that's right as far as the equations being  logistic beta = Z / sqrt(sum(eff_N/4)*MAF*(1-MAF)) and  SE = 1/sqrt(sum(eff_N/4)*MAF*(1-MAF)). Great catch! I think METAL outputs sum(eff_N), but you'll want to confirm that, which you would then divide by 4 in the context of these equations.

As far as the slight discrepancies between Z in your input and output file from munge, the reason for that is that munge backs out Z using the p-values in the summary statistics files, and then attaches a sign to it based on the effect column (whether that be a Z-statistic, beta, OR, etc.). So the difference should be attributable to rounding, and really minimal, but if you are seeing any larger differences let me know and we can take a look.

-Andrew

messages.subject: Re: Population prevalence
messages.body_plain:
I'd say that it isn't a "downside" per se, but it is a bit pointless/futile. As the whole point of providing a population prevalence is to facilitate liability scale conversion, because clinically ascertained samples tend to have an inflated number of cases, which creates an upward bias in heritability estimates (and any downstream metrics which would incorporate heritability into its calculation). So if you don't have a population prevalence, setting it to equal the sample prevalence is just going to get you your estimates on the observed rather than the liability scale. And the extent of this biasing will be exacerbated, the bigger the discrepancy between the sample prevalence and the population prevalence (i.e. a sample prev of 40% and a pop prev of 30% will be less of a biased inflation than 40% sample prev, 0.1% pop prev). Out of curiosity, what is the phenotype?
